title: Food Rules Across Faiths
objective: After this level you can compare kosher, halal, Hindu, Jain and Buddhist food rules and the reasons each tradition gives for them.
summary: Kosher and halal rules rest on scripture and God's command; Hindu, Jain and Buddhist food customs grow from ahimsa, not harming living beings, practiced with very different strictness.

cards.headline: Why would a faith care what's on your plate?
cards.body: Kosher, halal, vegetarian, no onions: food rules are among religion's most visible habits. Line them up and two very different kinds of reason appear.

cards.headline: Kosher: because God commanded it
cards.body: Jewish dietary law permits mammals that chew the cud and have cloven hooves, and fish with both fins and scales. So no pork and no shellfish. Meat and dairy are kept strictly apart. The rules come from the Torah, in books such as Leviticus and Deuteronomy. And the reason? For observant Jews, Britannica notes, no motive is needed beyond God's command.

cards.headline: Halal: the permitted
cards.body: Halal means what Islamic law permits, and haram what it forbids. Pork, alcohol, blood and animals found dead are prohibited, and the slaughterer invokes God's name. Whether a food is halal is judged from the Quran and the Hadith, with analogy and scholarly consensus: the same sources as the rest of Islamic law. Two faiths, one logic: the rule comes from revelation.

cards.headline: Hindu and Jain tables: harm less
cards.body: India's traditions give a second reason: do no harm. Taught by Jains and Buddhists, that ideal was taken up in Hinduism and applied especially to the cow. In a Pew survey of India published in 2021, 44% of Hindus said they were vegetarian. Jains go furthest: 92% said so, and 67% avoid root vegetables, because pulling up roots destroys the whole plant.

cards.headline: The Buddhist alms bowl
cards.body: Buddhism's first precept is to refrain from taking life, yet practice varies. Early monks and nuns ate the alms they were given, refusing only animals slaughtered specifically for them. Vegetarian meals became the norm in Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monasteries, while in Theravada and Tibetan Buddhism vegetarianism is a personal choice.

cards.headline: Food Rules Across Faiths: the takeaways
learned: Kosher and halal rules rest on God's command in scripture
Hindu and Jain food customs grow from not harming living beings
Buddhist practice ranges from alms of any kind to strict vegetarianism

questions.prompt: Match each term or group with what this level says about it.
questions.explanation: Halal is what Islamic law permits and haram what it forbids. Kosher law permits fish with both fins and scales, and many Jains avoid root vegetables.

questions.prompt: A Jain family skips potatoes; a Jewish family skips shrimp. Which pair of reasons fits each family best?

options.label: Jain: health; Jewish: cost
options.rationale: Neither tradition gives these as its reason.

options.label: Jain: avoiding harm to living things; Jewish: God's command
Jain: God's command; Jewish: avoiding harm
Both: rules set by the state
options.rationale: Both rules are religious, not state law.

questions.explanation: Jains avoid root vegetables because uprooting kills the whole plant; kosher rules rest on God's command.

questions.prompt: Kosher and halal rules both forbid pork. Their two faiths belong to which family from Level 8?

options.label: The Indian family
options.rationale: That family includes Hinduism and Jainism.

options.label: The East Asian family
options.rationale: That's Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist and Shinto.

questions.explanation: Judaism and Islam, with Christianity, share reverence for Abraham: the Abrahamic family.
